title: Capstone Walkthrough: Engagement Tiers
objective: After this lesson you will be able to combine ranking, NTILE tiers, LAG deltas, running aggregates, and FILTER metrics into one staged cohort-style analysis — and present it as cited findings with caveats, ready for the final assessment and your capstone.
why: Window courses often end at function reference; analysts end at narratives. This walkthrough fuses all five lessons on one question — 'who are our learners, really?' — into tiered, ranked, delta-measured findings. It is the worked example your capstone mirrors and the closest thing to a real analytics deliverable this platform teaches.

blocks.text: *'Segment our developers by engagement and tell us who leads, who lags, and where the gaps are.'* Three analytic cuts: (1) **tiers** — NTILE quartiles by hours (who sits where); (2) **gaps** — LAG deltas between consecutive learners (where are the cliffs?); (3) **context** — role averages attached to every row (is a lagging learner actually above their role?). Each cut is one lesson; the report is their fusion.

Quartile everyone by hours studied: NTILE(4) over descending hours. The tier table is the report's skeleton — every later finding hangs a row on it. Persist the tier labels with the analysis date: recomputed quartiles drift as data grows (Ch.2 remainder rules), and undated tiers are unactionable.

blocks.code:
-- Tier skeleton: every learner, labeled (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, role, hours_studied,
  NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS tier
FROM developers
ORDER BY hours_studied DESC;
blocks.caption: NTILE tiers: the report's skeleton (14 rows: 4,4,3,3)

blocks.text: Gaps between consecutive learners expose cliffs: a 200-hour drop between ranks 3 and 4 means the top tier stands apart. LAG over the same ordering, differenced, ordered by gap descending — the biggest structural breaks surface first. Cliffs justify tier boundaries better than arbitrary cutoffs.

blocks.code:
-- Cliff hunt: biggest drops between consecutive learners (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  LAG(hours_studied, 1) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS prev_hours,
  LAG(hours_studied, 1, hours_studied) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) - hours_studied AS cliff
FROM developers
ORDER BY cliff DESC;
blocks.caption: LAG deltas ordered by size: structural breaks first

blocks.text: A bottom-quartile fullstack developer above the fullstack average is a different story than one below it. Attach `AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY role)` to every row (Ch.1 shape) and flag the mismatch tier-vs-context explicitly — findings with this structure ('Q3 overall, above role average') are the ones stakeholders quote.

blocks.code:
-- Full fusion: tier + cliff + role context in one staged query
-- (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
-- WITH tiered AS (
--   SELECT name, role, hours_studied,
--     NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS tier,
--     AVG(hours_studied) OVER (PARTITION BY role) AS role_avg
--   FROM developers
-- )
-- SELECT name, role, hours_studied, tier,
--   ROUND(role_avg, 1) AS role_avg,
--   CASE WHEN hours_studied >= role_avg THEN 'above role' ELSE 'below role' END AS vs_role
-- FROM tiered ORDER BY hours_studied DESC;
blocks.caption: Fusion: three lessons, one staged query, quotable rows

blocks.title: Findings, not rows
blocks.text: The deliverable is sentences with citations, not result dumps: 'The top tier (4 learners, 783h+) stands 200h+ clear of tier 2 (cliff Q); two Q3 learners sit above their role averages — coaching candidates, not at-risk.' Every clause traces to a query; small samples carry caveats.

blocks.query: SELECT MIN(hours_studied) AS lo, MAX(hours_studied) AS hi, COUNT(*) AS n FROM developers;
blocks.note: Run this range snapshot in the sandbox — the span your tiers slice and your cliffs dissect. Tier widths and cliff sizes mean nothing without the total range in mind: ground every window finding in flat descriptives first.

items: Tier (NTILE) for structure, gaps (LAG) for cliffs, context (partition averages) for meaning — fuse all three
Persist tier labels with dates; recomputed quantiles drift
Flag tier-vs-context mismatches explicitly — they are the quotable findings
Deliver cited sentences with caveats, never raw result dumps

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, run the range snapshot plus the per-role GROUP BY baseline; record both. (b) In real SQLite/PostgreSQL, build the three cuts (tiers, cliffs, fusion with vs_role flags). (c) Write three finding bullets in the quotable style (tier + cliff/context + caveat), each citing its cut.
hints: Baselines first: range (MIN/MAX/COUNT) plus role averages — every window number below must be reconcilable with these flats.
Cuts mirror the lesson code: NTILE tiering, LAG cliff ordered DESC, fusion CTE with CASE vs_role. Verify tier sizes (4,4,3,3) and cliff arithmetic by hand on two rows.
Bullet shape: claim (numbers) + cut citation + caveat. Example: 'Tier 1 holds 4 learners above 780h (cut 1); the tier1→2 cliff exceeds 100h (cut 2); n=14 total, treat tier edges as approximate.'
exercise.solution:
-- (b) three cuts (real SQLite / PostgreSQL — see lesson code)
-- tiers: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC)
-- cliffs: LAG difference ordered DESC
-- fusion: tier + AVG OVER (PARTITION BY role) + CASE vs_role
-- (c) example bullets: tier composition (cut 1), biggest cliff (cut 2),
-- above-role Q3 learners (cut 3) — each with n-caveats.
exercise.why: The exercise performs the analyst loop at capstone scale: flat grounding, staged window analysis, cited prose with caveats. Queries are evidence; sentences are the product — rehearsed here, graded in the project.

quiz.q: Why persist NTILE tier labels with their analysis date?
options: Recomputed quantiles drift as data grows — undated tiers from different runs are incomparable
quiz.explain: Quantile boundaries move with the data (remainder rules + growth). A 'Q1 learner' means nothing without as-of dating — comparability requires versioning.

quiz.q: A 200-hour gap between ranks 3 and 4 justifies tier boundaries better than arbitrary cutoffs because…
options: Cliffs are data-structural breaks: the distribution itself separates there, rather than an analyst's round number
quiz.explain: Distribution-led segmentation (cliffs) beats analyst-imposed cutoffs: boundaries sit where the data actually breaks, making tiers defensible rather than decorative.

quiz.q: A Q3 learner sits above their role average. Correct reporting?
options: Flag the mismatch explicitly: below overall, above role — a coaching candidate with context, not a plain laggard
quiz.explain: Tier-vs-context mismatches are the quotable findings: single-metric labels mislead where fused signals inform. Report both, interpret the tension.

quiz.q: Report shows result tables without sentences. What's missing?
options: Findings: cited claims with caveats — queries are evidence, sentences are the product
quiz.explain: Stakeholders decide on sentences, not dumps. Every bullet traces to a cut; small samples carry caveats. That is the analyst's deliverable.

summary: Tier for structure, gaps for cliffs, role context for meaning — fused in staged windows, delivered as cited, caveated sentences. Course complete: assessment, then the leaderboard-and-tiers capstone.
